doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: Leading an orchestra at The Pines Hotel in 1931 and learning of Casa Loma
summary: Budd's last professional gig, his aunt's help, his band at Digby, and the violinist who told them about Casa Loma.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Were you a fan of the big bands during the 40’s?

Oh yes, yes indeed. The first real big band that impressed me that I knew anything about was Casa Loma. I had an orchestra in The Pines Hotel in Digby, Nova Scotia, which is CPR Hotel in 1931, my third year in medical school. And one of the interesting things about that, I don’t know whether it should be publicized or not, but my aunt, that Marjorie knows of course, was very helpful to me in everything I did. She gave me my first blood pressure machine when I was a medical student. She also was around St. Stephen when I was born. And she arranged for me to get an externship in a place in New York, Brownsville, New York. I don’t know, but somebody tells me it’s a pretty tough section now. But she said “you’ve got a job working as an extern in the emergency room there this summer.” 1931. In that same year I got the opportunity to get an orchestra and go and play in The Pines Hotel in Digby. That would be my last big shot at professional playing. And I had to write and tell Aunt Bess I wasn’t feeling well or something and tell the hospital that I was too ill, I couldn’t come. So I went to The Pines Hotel. And we had a saxophone player — two of them — my roommate that taught me so much, and another saxophone player from Halifax, and a drummer that was not a medical student but he played in so many bands at the college that even the professors thought he was a student, and a piano, and we had to have a violin. And I knew nobody in Halifax except some of the girls perhaps that could play violin really in tune. I knew Joe Venuti by hearing him but I said nobody can play like that. But I did get a man from a friend named Milton Karasek, who was from Boston. And we got in touch with him and he’d come down and work with us and play. He came over on a boat and you weren’t allowed to come in as a job so he had his violin and he had some other guy with a suitcase and he gave the violin © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

to another passenger to take it off and carry with the suitcase so they’d have no trouble with customs. But he was a great musician. And he was the one who said “have you fellas ever heard of the Casa Loma orchestra?” And we hadn’t and he just was so enthralled, and he said “you should hear them.” And then that was my first big band.
